Hilbert space. A Hilbert space is a complete vector space equipped with an inner product, a generalization of Euclidean space to infinite dimensions. More formally, it's a complete, separable inner product space where "complete" means all Cauchy sequences converge and "inner product" provides a notion of angle and length. Hilbert spaces are the natural mathematical setting for quantum mechanics, signal processing, and functional analysis, enabling rigorous treatment of infinite-dimensional linear systems.

Here's what defines a Hilbert space. A Hilbert space H is a vector space with an inner product, a function that takes two vectors and produces a number. This inner product generalizes the familiar dot product: it measures the correlation between vectors, satisfying linearity, conjugate symmetry, and positive-definiteness. The norm—written as the square root of the inner product of a vector with itself—measures length. The distance between two vectors is the norm of their difference. Vectors are orthogonal when their inner product is zero; an orthonormal basis consists of orthogonal unit vectors that span the space. Most importantly, the space is complete: every Cauchy sequence converges to a limit in the space itself. This ensures that limits of approximating sequences don't escape the space.

Concrete examples help. The space of square-summable infinite sequences is a Hilbert space. So is the space of square-integrable functions on an interval. In both cases, the completeness property is what makes them Hilbert spaces rather than mere inner product spaces. Any element in a Hilbert space can be written as a convergent sum over an orthonormal basis, which generalizes Fourier decomposition. Linear operators on Hilbert spaces may have eigenvalues and eigenvectors, and the spectral theorem ensures that Hermitian operators can be diagonalized.

Hilbert spaces emerged from David Hilbert's work on integral equations in the early twentieth century and were formalized by von Neumann and others in the 1920s and 1930s. They provided the rigorous mathematical foundation for quantum mechanics: the state of a quantum system is a vector in a Hilbert space, observables are Hermitian operators, and measurement outcomes are eigenvalues. Quantum field theory is built entirely on operator algebras on Hilbert spaces. Beyond physics, Hilbert spaces underpin functional analysis, signal processing with wavelets and Fourier analysis, machine learning via kernel methods, and approximation theory. Most of modern mathematical physics and analysis is conducted in the language of Hilbert spaces.
